summary: Bloomberg's Tom Maloney uses exhibits from Donald Trump's New York civil fraud trial to compare Trump's 2021 valuations, New York State's figures and Bloomberg's own estimates for four properties: Mar-a-Lago, the Trump Tower penthouse, Trump Park Avenue and 40 Wall Street. Trump's 2021 statement pegged his net worth at $US4.5 billion, while Bloomberg's calculations have consistently come in lower. The article details alleged inflations such as the penthouse's size and rent-stabilised apartment values, though Bloomberg values some properties higher than the state does.
one_line: Bloomberg compares Trump's, New York State's and its own valuations of four key Trump properties amid the New York civil fraud trial.
key_facts: Trump's 2021 statement of financial condition, filed in the lawsuit, pegged his net worth at $US4.5 billion; Bloomberg's calculation has consistently been below Trump's figures.
Trump testified that banks didn't rely on his financial statements, saying they "just weren't a very important element in banks' decision-making process."
Mar-a-Lago was valued at $US612.1 million by Trump (2021), $US240 million by Bloomberg (2023) and $US27.6 million by New York (2021).

Trump agreed with Palm Beach County and the National Trust for Historic Preservation that Mar-a-Lago be used only as a club, giving up development rights, so the county assessed it as a business at $US27.6 million in 2021.
Mar-a-Lago took in about $US41 million in revenue last year versus $US21 million in 2019, per Trump's most recent ethics disclosure.
Between 2011 and 2016 Trump valued his Trump Tower penthouse as 30,000 square feet, almost triple its actual 10,996 square feet.
Trump raised the penthouse value to $US327 million from $US200 million between 2014 and 2015; Judge Arthur Engoron wrote in a September ruling that such a discrepancy 'can only be considered fraud'.
The penthouse was valued at $US131.3 million by Trump (2021) and $US40 million by Bloomberg (2023); New York has no current estimate.
Trump Park Avenue was valued at $US90.9 million by Trump, $US86.4 million by Bloomberg and $US80 million by New York.
In 2010, 12 rent-stabilised Trump Park Avenue apartments were appraised at an average of $US62,500 each; the next year Trump valued them at $US4.1 million each, over 65 times greater.
By 2021 only five of those 12 apartments remained rent stabilised.

40 Wall Street was valued at $US664 million by Trump (2021) and $US270 million by Bloomberg (2023); it was appraised at $US200 million in 2011 and $US220 million in 2012 while Trump used $US524.7 million and $US527.2 million.
40 Wall Street occupancy slid to 77 per cent in June from 98 per cent in 2015, and net operating income is only 61 per cent of underwriters' projections.
The 40 Wall Street ground lease resets in 2032 and would jump to $US30 million from about $US2.6 million at current rent.
